<reason>CON fought the sharper tactical war — the "records tell you how much, not why" attack, the thermometer line, the contradiction that PRO's records were sold as the fix for both pandemic failures and then reframed as coverage-only, the late arrival of a named payer (with the awkward "general revenue" admission), the algorithmic-starvation case where no separation event exists, and the reclassification counterplan with its foreclosure claim. On the UI branch specifically CON is ahead, helped by the genuinely apt observation that contributory schemes typically cover the self-employed for pensions and sickness but exclude them from UI precisely because the insured controls the event. But the motion as written spans UI *and* broader social-insurance eligibility, and PRO's structural split was the decisive move of the debate. CON explicitly conceded that for pensions, sickness, injury and parental cover "eligibility really is a contribution record," and then had to defend that branch with "the record is decoration" — a weak answer, since without counted earnings there are no credits to decorate. PRO also neutralized CON's core framing by noting that no UI system asks earnings records to adjudicate separation; records set base-period coverage, a separate determination sets cause. That leaves CON needing the foreclosure argument (a contractor track kills misclassification enforcement) to sink the whole motion, and it arrived late, remained speculative, and was partly blunted by PRO's point that any reclassification remedy still runs on the same measured earnings data. PRO's decision rule — "compare imperfect adjudication to invisibility; a partial benefit imperfectly awarded beats zero perfectly administered" — survived. PRO's two clipped over-length turns are a real execution cost, and CON's prose was tighter and more memorable, which keeps this competitive rather than comfortable.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's [A2.4]–[A2.6] division-of-labor rebuttal: earnings records establish coverage and benefit level while a separate determination adjudicates cause, so CON "has discovered that a thermometer doesn't diagnose the illness." Combined with the observation that CON offered no objection at all to counting platform earnings toward pensions, sickness, injury and parental cover, this reframed CON's central objection as an argument for better adjudication rules rather than against the motion — and CON's later fallback that "for pensions the record is decoration" was the weakest link in an otherwise sharp CON case.</best_rebuttal>
